pitchHistory.title: The Inference Wall: Why Scaling Laws Just Hit Their First Real Speed Bump
pitchHistory.summary: In late 2025, something quietly broke the AI industry's founding assumption: that more compute reliably buys you smarter models. The frontier labs are now burning billions on inference-time compute — chain-of-thought, test-time scaling, 'thinking' models — because pre-training returns are diminishing faster than anyone publicly admitted. This post unpacks what the engineering reality actually looks like, why it matters that we're shifting from a training-compute race to an inference-compute race, and what that means for who gets to build competitive AI systems in 2026 and beyond.

pitchHistory.title: Vibe Coding Is Real Now — and It's Going to Break Something Important
pitchHistory.summary: Andrej Karpathy coined 'vibe coding' barely a year ago as a half-joke, but in 2026 it's a genuine workflow: developers describe intent, AI writes the code, humans ship without fully reading what's underneath. This post digs into what that actually means for software quality, security, and the long-term craft of engineering — not with moral panic, but with a clear-eyed look at which risks are overblown and which ones should genuinely keep you up at night.

pitchHistory.title: The CPU Is Back. Blame the Agents.
pitchHistory.summary: For five years, every AI infrastructure conversation started and ended with GPUs. Now Nvidia — of all companies — is telling us the CPU has become the bottleneck, and it's betting billions on its own Vera CPU to fix it. This post digs into why agentic AI workloads are fundamentally different from training runs, why the GPU-centric stack wasn't designed for them, and what this quiet architectural shift means for the next generation of AI infrastructure.

pitchHistory.title: The Scanners Are Compromised: What the Trivy Attack Tells Us About Trusting Our Own Tools
pitchHistory.summary: On March 19, 2026, attackers poisoned Trivy — one of the most widely used open-source vulnerability scanners — turning the tool that was supposed to protect CI/CD pipelines into the weapon that raided them: 76 of 77 release tags retroactively repointed, credentials silently stolen, a self-propagating worm seeded across npm. The counterintuitive horror here isn't just another supply chain breach — it's that we handed attackers a master key by concentrating so much pipeline trust into security tooling itself. This post unpacks how the attack worked, why 'verify your dependencies' breaks down when your verifier is the thing that's compromised, and what a genuinely hardened build pipeline has to look like now.
